sections.body: This field covers the practical work of turning AI research into funded projects. Artificial intelligence is now used to draft proposal text from prior papers, check formatting against funder rules, estimate budgets, suggest collaborators, and score a proposal's likely success. These tools read existing research, extract claims, and assemble sections that match a call's requirements. The work is not theoretical, systems are already producing drafts and compliance checks for researchers.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Drafting from past work is fairly reliable when source papers are clean and well structured, but generated text still needs human review for accuracy and fit. Compliance checking can catch missing sections and formatting errors, yet it often misses subtle agency requirements or changes in policy. Budget tools can list allowable costs from templates, but they cannot judge whether a cost is truly justified. Predicting success is the least solved area, models can rank proposals by similarity to funded ones, but they cannot account for reviewer taste, timing, or luck. Honest limits include poor performance on novel research ideas and a tendency to echo boilerplate.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with Drafting Proposals from Past Work to see how the site's 135 research papers and 10555 extracted claims can be turned into a first draft. Funder Formatting and Compliance then explains how to check that draft against a specific agency's rules. Budgets and Allowable Costs covers the financial side, including what a funder will and will not pay for. Finding Collaborators helps locate people whose past work matches the proposal's needs. Predicting Proposal Success closes the loop by estimating whether the finished proposal is likely to win, with all the caveats that such estimates carry.
